soil-bio-303.title: Why farmed soils hold less organic matter than pasture
soil-bio-303.text: In a New York study, pasture soils averaged 4.5% organic matter and conventional vegetable soils only 2.7%. The gap follows what each system returns to the ground. Cash grain farms sell 55-60% of their aboveground biomass and replace nutrients with fertilizer, but not carbon. Dairy farms return most biomass as manure, and organic vegetable farms import compost or manure. The study put annual grain at 2.9%, dairy at 3.4% and mixed vegetable at 3.9%. Aggregates followed the same order: the share of water-stable aggregates rose from 27% in conventional vegetable soils to 70% in no-till pasture. See {{ref:soil-bio-294}} for the balance behind it.

soil-bio-308.title: Five groups of soil health practices
soil-bio-308.text: Good soil management is not one trick but five families of them. Practices aimed at {{ref:soil-env-174}} should grow healthy plants, suppress pests or increase beneficial organisms, while reducing harm to the environment. They group into minimizing disturbance, keeping soil covered, maximizing biodiversity, managing water, and maintaining pH and nutrients without excessive loss. Organic matter practices come first for long-term sustainability, because each one has multiple benefits. Good physical condition and nutrient management still need additional practices.

soil-bio-313.title: What organic matter practices do for nutrients
soil-bio-313.text: A legume cover crop does several jobs at once. It adds active organic matter, cuts erosion and supplies nitrogen to the next crop. Cover and deep-rooted crops also cycle nitrate, potassium, calcium and magnesium that might otherwise leach away. Importing manure or compost adds nutrients too, but applied routinely every year it can overload the soil. Organic matter, the {{ref:soil-found-045}} the earlier entries described, does not settle everything. Testing manure, timing nutrients, liming and soil tests are separate practices that still have to be done.

soil-bio-297.title: How a crop rotation raises or drains organic matter
soil-bio-297.text: Organic matter rises and falls as a rotation moves from crop to crop. Perennial forages build it, while annual row crops under plowing deplete it. Hay and pasture crops add much root biomass and leave the soil undisturbed. Sod crops also cut erosion and residue decomposition. What a crop returns depends on the crop and the harvest: corn grain leaves more residue than soybean, wheat or silage harvest. Cover crops protect bare soil and add organic material, in amounts set by the cover type and its biomass before termination. This is the {{ref:soil-bio-294}} played out across several seasons.

soil-bio-296.title: How erosion strips organic matter and yield
soil-bio-296.text: Erosion takes the best soil first. Topsoil is rich in organic matter, so when water, wind or tillage carries it off, organic matter, water storage and yields all drop. Agricultural practice greatly speeds all three kinds of erosion, and in the United States the loss costs about $1 billion a year in available nutrients. Yields fall 5-10% under moderate erosion and 10-20% or more under severe erosion. On Corwin soil, between slight and severe erosion, organic matter fell from 3.03% to 1.86%. Available water capacity fell from 12.9% to 6.6%, roughly halving. That is the {{ref:soil-found-045}} paying for the topsoil that left.

soil-bio-298.title: Manure and other amendments from off the field
soil-bio-298.text: Bringing manure or other organic residues onto a field helps maintain or even raise its organic matter. The amounts can be large. A Vermont study found that 20-30 tons per acre of wet dairy manure were needed every year to maintain organic matter under continuous silage corn. The effects depend on manure type, on storage and handling, and on whether it is spread on the surface or incorporated. Nitrogen is a different tool. Synthetic nitrogen raises yields and residue, but it is often applied up to 50% above what the plants need.

soil-bio-310.title: Should crop residues be burned as fuel?
soil-bio-310.text: Crop residues look like free fuel, but soil also wants them. Using residues as biofuel feedstock could starve the soil of the organic inputs that maintain its quality. Most aboveground corn residue must return to the soil: an estimated 2-5 tons are needed to keep favourable properties. A long-term New York study found that modest cornstalk removal caused limited extra deterioration under no-till. Even so, routine removal calls for caution, most of all on cash grain fields with conventional tillage and no manure or compost. In 1980 Hans Jenny argued against indiscriminate conversion of biomass and organic wastes to fuels, because the humus capital deserves to be maintained. The question is still weighed case by case, and the evidence on how much removal soil can tolerate is limited.

soil-bio-312.title: Why farms with animals keep more organic matter
soil-bio-312.text: Farms with animals hold organic matter more easily, because manure recycles carbon and nutrients from feed grown on the farm. Integrating crops and livestock can start an upward spiral. Manure improves the soil, the crops then produce more residue and feed, and more animals mean more manure. Pasture, hay and haylage give perennial forages an economic use in the rotation. A farm with no animals can still obtain manure by trading hay with neighbors.

soil-bio-311.title: Which practices help water soak in
soil-bio-311.text: A field that takes in rain cuts runoff and erosion, refills the root zone and recharges groundwater. So which practices raise {{ref:soil-water-180}}? A University of Nebraska review of 89 studies found that perennial grass or legume hay and cover crops gave the greatest gains. No-till raised it only inconsistently. It worked when combined with surface residues and cover crops.

soil-bio-305.title: How much organic material it takes to gain 1 percent
soil-bio-305.text: Raising soil organic matter by 1% sounds modest, but it takes a very large addition of material. The top 6 inches of soil weigh about 2 million pounds, so 1% organic matter in that layer is 20,000 pounds. Most of what is added never stays, because decomposers consume it. If 80% is lost and 20% ends up as stable organic matter, roughly 100,000 pounds (50 tons) of dry organic material is needed for each 1% gain. That is the arithmetic behind {{ref:soil-found-045}} changing slowly.

soil-bio-291.title: Why acidic soils pile up organic matter on top
soil-bio-291.text: Organic matter breaks down more slowly in acidic soil than near neutral pH. One reason is earthworms: acidity inhibits them. Without them, organic matter accumulates at the surface instead of being mixed through the soil layers. {{ref:soil-found-014}} therefore shapes where the organic matter sits as well as how much of it there is.

soil-bio-314.title: Forests, farmland and soil carbon
soil-bio-314.text: Cutting down a forest typically lowers its soil carbon, and planting trees again may partly restore the original levels. The rate varies. Boreal reforestation gains carbon more slowly than other climates because trees grow slowly, and the previous land use and the type of disturbance control the rate. Afforested farmland gains more soil carbon than pasture or grassland, and mine-disturbed soils also gain a lot. Where they suit the site, deciduous trees raise soil carbon faster than conifers. Over time they also store more of it in the mineral soil than in the forest floor.

soil-bio-299.title: Where organic matter sits in aggregates
soil-bio-299.text: Organic matter lives both outside and inside soil crumbs. Outside aggregates it is roots, organisms and residue. Inside them it is adsorbed on clay and small silt, or trapped in small aggregates. Organic matter inside very small aggregates is out of reach of microorganisms and enzymes, and it also helps bind mineral particles. Larger aggregates are held mainly by fungal hyphae and their secretions, other microbial products, and roots. Tiny pores inside them can shelter microbes from predators. Finer soils need more of it: for over half of aggregates to be water-stable, a 50% clay soil may need twice the organic matter of a 10% clay soil.

soil-bio-320.title: When carbonates fool a carbon test
soil-bio-320.text: A soil test can report more organic carbon than the soil really holds. Carbonates decompose to CO2 during combustion-based analysis, and the instrument counts that CO2 as organic carbon. The problem arises on limestone-derived soils, including surface soils where tillage erosion has exposed carbonate-rich horizons. Three approaches separate carbonate carbon from organic carbon: heat treatment, acid treatment and wet oxidation.

soil-bio-289.title: Why wet and low places collect organic matter
soil-bio-289.text: In a Florida drained peatland, some homes now stand on posts above a surface that has sunk. Poor aeration slows decomposition, so organic matter accumulates in wet soils and low landscape positions. Lignin does not decompose at all without oxygen. Very long wetness produces peat or muck soils with over 20% organic matter. Draining those soils reverses the effect: the organic matter decomposes rapidly and the surface sinks. The landscape matters as well. Depressions and floodplains collect runoff, sediment and organic matter, so they accumulate more, while steep slopes and knolls stay low because topsoil keeps eroding. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-317.title: Measuring carbon and nitrogen by burning the soil
soil-bio-317.text: Dry combustion measures carbon by burning it. A ground soil sample is burned in oxygen, and the CO2 and nitrogen released give total carbon and nitrogen together. Samples under 250 μm are burned at about 1250°C. Copper at 600°C reduces nitrogen oxides to N2, and a gas chromatograph separates CO2 from N2 for detection. To get organic carbon alone, carbonates are removed by acid, measured by neutralization, or avoided by burning at 860°C, which decomposes only organic carbon.

soil-bio-315.title: Why some organic matter lasts and some vanishes
soil-bio-315.text: Under aerobic conditions, microbes respire organic inputs to carbon dioxide and water, using oxygen as the electron acceptor. How fast they do it depends on the chemistry of the input. Cellulose breaks into simple sugars that are readily degraded. Lignin, a network of aromatic components, is hard to break down and is mainly degraded by fungi. More complex organic matter needs more chemical energy and oxygen to degrade, which is one reason it persists longer. Fresh plant residue can fuel microbial activity that degrades stored carbon, an effect called priming, or it can add to stored carbon. The outcome depends on input quality, microbes, oxygen, water and time. Respiration is much slower without oxygen, so conversion of plant carbon takes longer in anaerobic soils. Compare {{ref:soil-bio-115}}.
